claims.quote: The study's door was locked from the inside, and every window in that room was latched.
The study's door was locked from the inside, and every window in that room was latched.
Victor Hale lay in his study as if his last conversation had been with the fabric of his own chair.
"Victor's heavy upholstered study chair — the site where he was found slumped. It bears old repairs and a faint circular wear spot on the left rear seam."

On his person lay his watch — gold, small, ruined in one graceful way: "Victor's gold pocket watch found stopped on his person; the minute hand bent and the watch stopped at a time relevant to establishing the minute of death."
The watch had indeed stopped. The minute hand had been bent; the watch read 9:14 p.m.

"The mantel clock, a gilt 19th-century piece, chimes every quarter-hour; its mechanism was Victor's pride." It chimes in the old pattern — one at the quarter, two at the half, three at the three-quarters, four on the hour — and in the hall the chime had already marked the evening for us once.

the draft of a new will had been found on Victor's desk and it suggested he intended to cut someone out — "A draft copy of Victor's new will, suggesting he intended to cut someone out; its existence supplies motive."
There was, on inspection, no conventional weapon in the room. Whoever had done this had left no knife on the carpet, no blunt instrument on the desk: only the body and its last arrangements.

The study itself offered a handful of physical cues that I filed in the order my hands could reach them: a faint abrasion at the chair frame, dust pressed and tufted where someone had shifted, a bent minute hand on a dead watch that read 9:14, and the worn, circular spot on the left rear seam of the chair where a pocket or a shoulder might have rubbed for years.

In the foyer the household and the night's guests had been gathered. Lucy Hale stood by the newel, hands clasped so tight the knuckles showed white; she was plainspoken in her grief and in her fear — inheritance anxiety, you could call it, though that is a small thing when a man is dead.
Alfred Broome, the butler, kept his face nearly blank; the stoic, old-school air of a man who has spent his life managing other people's exactness.
Owen Myers hovered, aggrieved and quick to snap a remark; he is a clock repairman and collector, skilled with small mechanisms and apt to quarrel with Victor over the worth of a thing.
Evelyn Ross smiled with the thin courtesy of business; she was the collector who wanted what Victor kept, every polite syllable counting toward acquisition.
I tell you this because detail is the only thing that steadies you in a room where someone has just stopped being anything at all.
